topic.subject: social
topic.title: Markets around us
topic.scope: weekly markets, shops, malls, chain of markets, wholesale and retail, market and equality

misconceptions.statement: Weekly markets are only for poor people.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the lower prices and lack of permanent infrastructure in weekly markets and associate these with poverty.
misconceptions.fix: Weekly markets offer goods at lower prices because they have fewer overhead costs, making them accessible and useful for people of all income levels.

probe.question: Why would a wealthy person choose to buy vegetables from a weekly market instead of a mall?
probe.wrong_answer: They wouldn't, because weekly markets are meant only for those who cannot afford expensive shops.

misconceptions.statement: Malls are always better than local shops because they sell better quality products.
misconceptions.why: The clean, air-conditioned environment of malls creates a perception of superior quality compared to local shops.
misconceptions.fix: Malls and local shops often source goods from the same wholesale markets; the difference lies in the shopping experience and the services provided, not necessarily the quality of the product.

probe.question: If a shirt is sold in both a local shop and a mall, which one is of better quality?
probe.wrong_answer: The one from the mall is definitely better quality because malls only keep high-end goods.

misconceptions.statement: A wholesaler is just a shopkeeper who sells in bulk.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate the act of selling many items with the specific economic role of a wholesaler in the supply chain.
misconceptions.fix: A wholesaler acts as a middleman who buys goods in large quantities directly from producers and sells them to retailers, not directly to final consumers.

probe.question: Can you go to a wholesaler to buy a single packet of biscuits for your lunch?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are just big shops that sell everything in bulk to anyone who walks in.

misconceptions.statement: The price of a product is determined only by the cost of making it.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the production cost and ignore the added costs of transportation, storage, and profit margins of various intermediaries.
misconceptions.fix: The final price includes production costs plus the profits and expenses of wholesalers, transporters, and retailers who handle the product along the chain.

probe.question: Why does a pen cost more in a shop than it does at the factory?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the shopkeeper is cheating the customer by charging extra money for no reason.

misconceptions.statement: Everyone has an equal opportunity to earn money in the market.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe in a meritocratic view of markets where hard work alone guarantees success, ignoring structural inequalities.
misconceptions.fix: Access to capital, social networks, and resources varies greatly, meaning that small traders often struggle to compete with large businesses despite their hard work.

probe.question: If a small trader works as hard as a big business owner, will they both make the same profit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the market is fair and rewards everyone equally for their effort.
